Phase 3 — Visual Concept Study

The Record, warmed by the Open Door.

This is what the chosen direction actually looks like, built with Russ's real content — not another territory, not more prose. Territory A governs the structure. Territory B carries the voice, the portraiture, the human moments. Territory C shows up only where content is genuinely archival.

Before you scroll

Nothing here is built. Every screen below is a mockup — a labeled browser or phone frame — not a live page. Typefaces are Libre Baskerville (display) and Source Sans 3 (everything else, replacing Open Sans).

Colors, copy, and credentials are Russ's real numbers, pulled from app/content.tsx. Where I wrote new copy in Russ's voice, it's flagged as a draft for his review — not finished site copy.

Home Opening Variants

Two compositions for the first screen only, within the same visual language above — not new territories, just different weightings of typography versus portrait.

Variant A — Typography-led
ryanlegalpc.com
ExpertiseAboutPayment

Ryan Legal, PC — Fresno, California

Thirty-five years. One attorney. Direct access.

Russ Ryan represents employers, health centers, and non-profits in employment, health care, and business matters.

AV Preeminent Super Lawyer since 2014 90%+ record
Schedule a Consultation

Credibility leads. The headline itself carries the claim of experience; the portrait is a supporting thumbnail, not the opening's subject.

Variant B — Portrait-led
ryanlegalpc.com
ExpertiseAboutPayment

Meet Russ Ryan

Comfortable to talk to. Formidable when necessary.

Employment, health care, and business law for California employers and organizations.

AV Preeminent since 2012 9 reported appellate decisions
Schedule a Consultation

Warmth leads. Russ's face is the first thing a visitor sees; the credentials sit beside him as a quiet, confident list rather than a banner.

Evaluation

Variant B does more of the job in the first three seconds — a visitor lands on a real, specific person, not an abstract law-firm headline, which is the whole point of "direct access to Russ." Variant A reads more like the credibility side of the tension (formidable) and less of the approachable side.

Recommendation: lead Home with Variant B, but keep Variant A's headline strategy — write the actual headline as an experience claim ("thirty-five years, one attorney"), not a generic greeting, so the portrait doesn't have to carry credibility on its own.

Photography Strategy

The Open Door territory lives or dies on this. The good news: there's already a usable, real portrait in the repo. It just isn't environmental.

Fallback — Available Now

This is square-profile.webp, already in the repo — a genuine, well-lit studio portrait of Russ. It's a real asset, not stock, and it's strong enough to lead Home and About today if a new shoot doesn't happen before launch.

Placeholder — not a real photo"at his desk, mid-sentence, glasses off"

Intended — Future Session

An environmental portrait: Russ at his desk or in conversation, natural light, unposed. This frame is deliberately abstract — no photo exists yet, and faking one would misrepresent the office.

What a future session should capture:

  • An environmental portrait at Russ's actual desk, not a studio backdrop
  • Russ mid-conversation — listening, not posed for camera
  • Restrained office details: books, a real window, nothing staged
  • An identifiable feature of the Fresno office, if one exists (view, sign, entrance)
  • Working moments — reviewing a document, on the phone — never a courtroom pose
09

Motion & Interaction Notes

Restrained on purpose. Nothing here should compete with reading, and nothing essential should hide behind a hover.

Navigation150ms color/background fade on link hover; active route marked with a static gold underline, not a sliding indicator.
Anchor scrollingscroll-behavior: smooth for in-page jumps (About rail, this study's own nav) — instant under prefers-reduced-motion.
Section railDesktop: sticky, always visible. Mobile: horizontal scroll chips, current section marked by fill, not motion.
Progressive disclosureNative <details>/<summary> for long client and training lists — expands instantly, no accordion animation, keyboard-operable by default.
HoverBackground or underline only — no transform, scale, or shadow lift. Buttons lighten; text links underline.
FocusVisible 2px outline in gold or navy on every interactive element, never suppressed — required given the dense legal reference content.
Active / selectedSolid gold underline or left-border, not color inversion — keeps navy/gold pairing consistent across states.
Reduced motionAll transitions and smooth-scroll disabled under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce; nothing here depends on animation to convey state.
Mobile menuFull-height panel, fade only (no slide), traps focus while open, closes on Esc or outside tap.
Keyboard accessFull tab order through rail, disclosure widgets, and forms; disclosure content is real DOM, not hidden-until-JS.

Deliberately avoided

  • Ambient background animation
  • Scroll-triggered reveal effects
  • Parallax or scroll-linked motion
  • Hover-only disclosure of essential content
  • Animated counters on proof numbers
  • Page-load intro sequences
10

Critical Evaluation

Same rule as the audit: honest, not softened. Here's where this actually stands.

Working

Russ comes through, especially in Variant B and the About prototype

The portrait-led opening and the bio block do what the brief asked — a visitor meets a specific person within seconds, not a firm.

Watch

Still leans report-like in the archival blocks

Admissions and Positions tables are honest and scannable, but they're the least "Open Door" part of the system. That's intentional — but if Russ reacts to it as cold, that's the section to soften first, not the whole page.

Working

Navy/gold reads warmer than the current site without changing the anchors

Warm paper background and the deeper navy-deep tone do most of the work — the brand colors themselves didn't need to move.

Working

Libre Baskerville stays rare

It only appears in headlines, the practice index numerals, quotes, and case names. Everything else — including every subheading in the About prototype — is Source Sans 3. It never becomes the paragraph font anywhere in this study.

Working

Source Sans 3 earns its spot

Against Libre Baskerville's period character, it reads current without feeling trendy, and its numerals hold up in the citation and admissions tables — the actual test the brief set for it.

Watch

Cohesion with the physical sign depends on the logo file, which is untouched

The logo itself is unchanged and still reads correctly on both navy and paper. The open question is whether Libre Baskerville headlines feel like a deliberate relative of the logo's serif "R" and wordmark, or just "a serif" — that's worth Russ's eye directly, not just mine.

Working

Proof is visible without being boastful

The proof strip and inline chips state facts (AV Preeminent, 90% record, 9 decisions) without adjectives doing the selling — no "award-winning," no exclamation points.

Working

Both institutional and personal visitors can orient

A health-center GC scanning for compliance experience and an individual worried about a wrongful-termination claim both hit real, specific proof within the first screen or two — neither audience has to dig.

Working

Reads as one attorney and a small office, not a firm

No "our attorneys," no "team" language anywhere in this study. Crystal is named once, specifically, for logistics — which is more honest than an anonymous "our staff."

Open Question

Every quote attributed to Russ here is a draft

I wrote his first-person lines from his real bio content, but they're mine until he reads and edits them. Nothing quoted in this study should be treated as approved copy.

Open Question

Confidentiality language on Contact is placeholder, pending his legal review

The note is directionally right but the exact wording needs Russ's sign-off before it goes anywhere near a live form.

Does this look and feel like Ryan Legal, PC?

Closer than the current site, and closer than either territory alone would have gotten. What's left before implementation isn't a design problem — it's getting Russ's actual words into the draft quotes and confidentiality copy, and deciding whether the archival blocks need one more pass of warmth or whether that restraint is exactly the point.
